[Film still.] Single-channel video projection shot on 16 mm Kodak Vision 3 500T film, wire gauze, plaster, cardboard, found objects, acrylic paint, confetti, wood, image prints, and celluloid film. 12 min 30 sec. A Secret Portrait of Wan Hoi-Ling (2025) reimagines the life of Wan Hoi-Ling, a pioneering but little-known female director and screenwriter who worked across Hong Kong and Singapore, creating anti-imperialist, anti-colonial films. In this interview, artist Elsa Wong reflects on how she transposed her research into the film’s three-part narrative, working with a variety of materials and techniques, from sourcing found objects to crafting dioramas, experimenting with 16mm film, and developing a multi-language soundtrack. Seeking an alternative to stereotypical portrayals of Wan as a tragic heroine, Elsa offers the viewer an empathetic vision of a woman moving through love, ambition, and loss. TO SEE Asian Film Archive: Edward Yang’s Four Favourite Films Following up from a full retrospective of […] As 2024 comes to an end, this issue of the Asian Cinema Digest highlights available screenings for the holiday season, as well as best-of lists, opinion pieces and reflective interviews to sum up our cinema journey this year. TO SEE Image still from Blue Velvet (1986, David Lynch) Asian Film Archive: Edward Yang’s Four Favourite Films Following up from a full retrospective of Edward Yang’s iconic oeuvre, the Asian Film Archive (AFA) presents 4 of the auteur’s favourite classic films: Nostalghia (1983) by Andrei Tarkovsky), My American Uncle (1980) by Alain Resnais, Blue Velvet (1986) by David Lynch and Aguirre, the Wrath of God (1972) by Werner Herzog, each having influenced Yang’s attitudes and approaches to his own practice. source_title: Blueprints For An Ephemeral and Affective Experience
source_description: My first encounter with the Asian Film Archive (AFA) was completely serendipitous. When I was at the Cannes Film Festival in 2022, I was able to catch a screening of Mike de Leon’s Itim, as part of the Cannes Classics selection. Having seen many older films before, it was not my first time watching one […] My first encounter with the Asian Film Archive (AFA) was completely serendipitous. When I was at the Cannes Film Festival in 2022, I was able to catch a screening of Mike de Leon’s Itim , as part of the Cannes Classics selection. Having seen many older films before, it was not my first time watching one with a ‘restored’ label. The magic of film restoration did not fully dawn on me until I watched Itim though. I was dumbfounded by the beauty of the restoration carried out by the film restoration laboratory, L’Immagine Ritrovata, as the version that I watched a long time ago was blotchy and was of very low-quality. I found that the restoration had maintained the atmosphere and visual signature of the film while elevating the technical ingenuity of the camerawork. Image stills from Itim (1976, Mike de Leon) This screening of Itim , and the entire Cannes Classics programme, opened me up to the world of moving image heritage. It reminded me of what my secondary school history teacher emphasised on the importance of learning about the past, that history is crucial to navigating the present and future. source_description: This issue of the Asian Cinema Digest focuses on Southeast, East and West Asian cinema. Delve into the works of Vietnamese filmmakers such as Nguyễn Trinh Thi and Trinh Thi Minh Hà, and film and video installations of Tulapop Saenjaroen. To celebrate the Lunar New Year, revisit some works from Hong Kong Cinema available on […] This issue of the Asian Cinema Digest focuses on Southeast, East and West Asian cinema. Delve into the works of Vietnamese filmmakers such as Nguyễn Trinh Thi and Trinh Thi Minh Hà, and film and video installations of Tulapop Saenjaroen. To celebrate the Lunar New Year, revisit some works from Hong Kong Cinema available on Criterion Channel. Also featured are the works of West Asian directors Bahram Beyzaie, Otar Iosseliani and Sergei Parajanov. WATCH Images de Chine (1901-1904) by Auguste François Shot at the end of the Qing dynasty, French consul, Auguste François (aka 方苏雅) captured people’s daily life in the streets of Kunming, Yunnan, using a camera given by Léon Gaumont. Cinémathèque Française and the CNC heritage department have scanned the nitrate films footage captured by François. Stream it now on Cinémathèque Française’s online platform, Henri. source_description: Bophana Center in collaboration with French Institute and Center for Khmer Studies (CKS) launches a week-long screening event. Since 2007, October 27th has been set by UNESCO as the World Day for Audiovisual Heritage to spotlight archives institutions, giving them an opportunity to showcase their works in celebration of the world audiovisual heritage. During one […] Bophana Center in collaboration with French Institute and Center for Khmer Studies (CKS) launches a week-long screening event. Since 2007, October 27th has been set by UNESCO as the World Day for Audiovisual Heritage to spotlight archives institutions, giving them an opportunity to showcase their works in celebration of the world audiovisual heritage. During one week, Bophana Center and the Institut français du Cambodge are collaborating to offer, for the first time in Cambodia, public screenings of rare movies on Indochina which were recently restored by the French CNC (Centre national du cinéma et de l’image animée). This movie selection aims to share the history and memories of the people of Indochina and also to raise the question of people’s identity under colonialism. The screenings will start on the World Day for Audiovisual Heritage and will last for one week. On the 27th of October, for the opening screening, Bophana Center will welcome Dr. Henri Locard for a lecture on Indochina; and on the 4th of November, for the closing screening, Ms. Khuon Vichheka will give a lecture, “Battambang during WWII”....

Dua peristiwa ini beredar cepat di media sosial, menyisakan jejak visual yang lebih kuat dari narasi panjang. Imbasnya jelas: desain protes tidak lagi bergantung pada poster atau tipografi, tapi bisa lahir spontan dari warna, dari momen, dari fragmen keseharian yang berubah jadi simbol. Apakah simbol selalu harus berupa gambar? Keraguan ini muncul ketika kita melihat bahwa warna sesederhana itu dapat menjadi tanda perlawanan. Dua warna ini berubah menjadi simbol cair, lahir spontan dari tubuh sosial. Di titik ini, kita belajar bahwa subversi visual tak selalu berbentuk lambang warna pun bisa menjadi penanda resistensi. source_description: Asal-Usul Tulisan ini merupakan tawaran dalam mengelola pembelajaran formal desain komunikasi visual (DKV). Tawaran tersebut hasil dari pengalaman dalam memberi lokakarya desain layout dan mengampu kelas pilihan Desain Layout. Lokakarya desain layout yang saya berikan untuk pers mahasiswa. Lokakarya tersebut biasanya diikuti beberapa orang, terutama bagian layouter di media pers mahasiswa … Asal-Usul Tulisan ini merupakan tawaran dalam mengelola pembelajaran formal desain komunikasi visual (DKV). Tawaran tersebut hasil dari pengalaman dalam memberi lokakarya desain layout dan mengampu kelas pilihan Desain Layout. Lokakarya desain layout yang saya berikan untuk pers mahasiswa. Lokakarya tersebut biasanya diikuti beberapa orang, terutama bagian layouter di media pers mahasiswa dan redaksi. Biasanya tak lebih dari lima orang peserta dengan jumlah pertemuan lima hingga tujuh kali. Sebelum dibuka mata kuliah pilihan Desain Layout di tempat saya mengajar (DKV ISI Yogyakarta) pernah ada mata kuliah dengan nama Komputer Grafis. Dari namanya memperlihatkan jejak era pembelajarannya. Nama “Komputer Grafis” sudah ada sebelum saya bergabung di Prodi DKV ISI Yogyakarta (2005). Dalam pembelajaran Komputer Grafis ada tiga pilihan software yakni Adobe Photoshop, Quarkxpress yang kemudian menjadi Page Maker lalu Adobe InDesign, dan Adobe Illustrator. Singkatnya, nama “Komputer Grafis” menggambarkan pentingnya mahasiswa mempelajari software saat itu. Jalan beberapa tahun nama kuliah...

source_description: Sebuah telaah kemungkinan sejarah baru desain grafis di Normal Baru melalui pembacaan peristiwa-peristiwa sejarah dunia dan kaitannya dengan desain grafis. Tulisan ini mendasarkan pembacaannya pada buku Desain Grafis Indonesia Dalam Pusaran Desain Grafis Dunia (2015). “Peran desain grafis dalam aktivisme dapat lebih dalam daripada sekadar poster dan T-shirt,” kata antropolog desain … Sebuah telaah kemungkinan sejarah baru desain grafis di Normal Baru melalui pembacaan peristiwa-peristiwa sejarah dunia dan kaitannya dengan desain grafis. Tulisan ini mendasarkan pembacaannya pada buku Desain Grafis Indonesia Dalam Pusaran Desain Grafis Dunia (2015). “ Peran desain grafis dalam aktivisme dapat lebih dalam daripada sekadar poster dan T-shirt ,” kata antropolog desain Stanford Dori Tunstall. Desain grafis tidak hanya menyoal visual yang tangible , tapi juga tentang perancangan ‘nilai sosial’ yang disepakati bersama oleh suatu pergerakan aktivisme tanpa memberi sekat terhadap disiplin tertentu. Dalam ranah sosial, keprofesian desain memang bersinggungan dan berkombinasi dengan bidang maupun disiplin lain. Dan dalam sejarahnya, keprofesian desain grafis juga ‘hadir’ dalam peristiwa-peristiwa dunia, bahkan dalam taraf tertentu dapat memberi dampak nyata bagi perubahan sosial budaya masyarakat di berbagai belahan di dunia. source_description: Arief ‘Ayip’ Budiman Minggu malam saya terima berita duka tersebut dari chat grup komunitas kecil kami. Kaget, karena sebelumnya ada berita duka juga terkait kawan lama. Sesaat setelahnya saya berusaha mengingat sosok Ayip. Secara pribadi saya tidak begitu kenal, namun dalam jejaring kami di asosiasi, organisasi, dan media ternyata Ayip dan … Arief ‘Ayip’ Budiman Minggu malam saya terima berita duka tersebut dari chat grup komunitas kecil kami. Kaget, karena sebelumnya ada berita duka juga terkait kawan lama. Sesaat setelahnya saya berusaha mengingat sosok Ayip. Secara pribadi saya tidak begitu kenal, namun dalam jejaring kami di asosiasi, organisasi, dan media ternyata Ayip dan saya cukup banyak berinteraksi. Saya mengingatnya lagi. Terakhir saya bertemu beliau di Agustus 2015, pada acara International Conference of Creative Industry (ICCI), diselenggarakan di Denpasar, Bali. Saya diundang untuk membicarakan topik ‘mapping’ profesi desain grafis dan memperkenalkan Desain Grafis Indonesia-DGI, organisai yang saya bantu kelola. Ayip membicarakan kegiatan kreatif inisiatifnya, sebuah proyek film. Ia memulai presentasinya dengan mengutip Bung Karno: “Negeri kita kaya, kaya, kaya-raya, saudara-saudara. Berjiwa besarlah, berimagination. Gali! Bekerja! Gali! Bekerja! source_description: Across Europe, industry unions and trade journals shaped the professionalisation of graphic design between 1890 and 1930. Journals such as Typografia, Das Plakat, The Penrose Annual and Typographische Jahrbucher. The spread of ideas, progression of standards and ideals were often shared in the distribution of magazines published by industry unions and collectives. Organisations and professional communities including typographic and printing unions such as the Bund Deutscher Buchdrucker (BDB), the German Printers’ Association, The Nederlandse Typografenbond (Dutch Typographers’ Union), the American Institute of Graphic Arts (AIGA) and the International Typographical Union, alongside similar bodies across Europe supported professionalisation, education, and the dissemination of design standards. The rapid progression of design, technology, and visual style during this period was recorded in design annuals and specialist trade journals. These included the British Penrose Annual, the German Das Plakat and Typographische Jahrbücher and Typographische Mitteilungen, and the Czech journal Typografia, all of which provide invaluable insight into evolving international practices. These became not just printed sources of inspiration, but forums for testing ideas, sharing opinion, and advancing the professionalisation of the trade. source_description: Art Nouveau spread through magazine covers across Europe, from the German Jugend to the Czech Typografia, and regional variations shaped the movement’s visual style in print. In the early twentieth century, advances in print production and transportation made reproduction and international distribution far easier than before, allowing magazines to become one of the fastest and most effective carriers for the spread of ideas, styles, and visual information. Art Nouveau ‘s stylistic regional differences and use of ornamentation can be seen when studying the cover of periodicals from the movement’s prime years. Amongst some of the long-standing magazines includes the German magazine Jugend, the Czech trade journal, Typografia , published by the Czech Typographers’ Union and the German magazine, Deutsche Kunst Und Dekoration. Jugend was first published in 1896 and was founded in Munich by Georg Hirth. It was a weekly magazine and ‘originally intended to showcase German Arts and Crafts, but became famous for showcasing the German version of Art Nouveau instead’. Its covers were influential and with over two thousand issues it showcased a range of artists including Otto Eckmann, Hans Christiansen and Bruno Paul. Many of the cover designs featured ornamental typography that was illustrated to blend with the cover image. source_object_type: Advertising Design; Design Archive Feature; Ephemera; Members Only Content
source_medium: Advertising Design; Design Archive Feature; Ephemera; Members Only Content
source_description: A collection of matchbox labels from around the world. Graphic design history of one of advertising’s smallest and most overlooked formats. One of the smallest canvases in the history of advertising, matchbox labels were produced economically and at high volume. Varying in size from a postage stamp to a playing card, these modest formats demanded maximum visual clarity. The designers had to reduce ideas to flat colour, simple iconography, and type that could be read at a glance. The printing constraints were severe. Most labels were produced by lithography, often in limited colour runs and on cheap paper stock. This forced designers to produce refined and constrained graphic design in the industrial era. The first friction match is believed to have been sold in 1827, following several prototypes developed by John Walker, a pharmacist from Stockton-on-Tees. As matches spread across the world, so did the labels that housed them. By the mid-nineteenth century, match manufacture had become a significant industry, with factories across Europe, Asia, and America producing matches by the billion. With competition between manufacturers, the label was one of the few points of difference available. Like all packaging, it had to identify the brand, communicate safety information, and catch the eye, all within a rectangle small enough to fit in a pocket. Among the highest-output producers, Czechoslovakia, the Soviet Union, and India each developed their own distinct visual styles....

source_description: 40 examples of Czech typography from Typografia Vol. 18 (1907). Czech commercial printing at the crossroads of Art Nouveau and early modernism, with work by Otokar Císař, Method Kaláb, and Mořic Novotný. Typografia was a Czech typography and printing journal first published in Prague in 1888. I have collected over 400 issues and continue to source the remaining missing volumes for the archive. Each issue included finely printed supplementary sheets featuring decorative commercial printing specimens, business stationery, advertisements, and typographic layouts, offering valuable examples of contemporary Czech typography and commercial printing practice. I have scanned in at high-resolution fourty of the sample sheets from the eighteenth volume in 1907. Linear Art Nouveau Advertisement Designs for Jan Hryzal and Václav Staroch Printing Works Art Nouveau advertisement and commercial designs for Jan Hryzal of Prague and the printing works of Václav Staroch in Žižkov. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 7, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Adolf Dvořák at the Politika printing works in Prague. The restrained compositions and simplified geometric ornament reflect the decorative Art Nouveau and functional commercial typography. source_description: An overview of graphic design in 1900, exploring Art Nouveau, the Eckmann-Schrift typeface, the Steglitz Workshop, the Doves Press and more, illustrated with artefacts from the Design Reviewed archive. This is the first of a series of articles focusing on graphic design year by year, which I intend to go from 1900-2000.The series will be illustrated with artefacts from the archive, scanned inners (in which I don’t currently have any original material) and relevant quotes and reference for further reading. I will also be revisiting this series from time-to-time as I uncover more content and add further artefacts to the archive. The series will also help me find gaps in the archive, in which I feel documentation isn’t on the website, and information and key pieces to be uploaded and purchased as I go. Although 1900 was the first year I wanted to focus on, the previous few years had seen the emergence of the Art Nouveau movement , which is regarded as one of the first international art movements. It became an international style and had a major influence on the design of books, posters and typeface design. Across Europe its variations of style and terms include Jugendstil, Modernismo, Secession and Stile Floreale. source_title: From the Collection: Emigre Font Development Files
source_description: Donated along with their collection in 2016, Emigre’s font development files represent a rare comprehensive view of a digital type foundry’s process. After two years of work, the collection is now digitized in full, a world’s first for such an archive. A selection of objects will be made available to the public through the Online Archive . Archive and Self At the time I joined the project, a number of posters and magazines had already been digitized. Having worked mostly in cataloging and processing at the Archive—and before that as a student worker in the Heller Rare Book Room at Mills College—I was still relatively new to the imaging process. Digitization Archivist Ellis Martin suggested the Font Development Files as a good starting point; the objects were primarily flat works on paper and relatively similar in size, which allowed me to focus on the finer points of digitization while moving through a substantial collection. Process work for Base 9/12 . Process work is special because it provides us with a clearer idea of how typefaces are constructed. The journey from idea to finished object is rarely linear, and its methods are seldom made visible to audiences. The development files contain a range of marked proofs, references, and revisions; correspondences between designers and collaborators; and mail from readers of Emigre magazine. Some of my favorite reference material appears in the “ Mrs Eaves ” folder, which includes photocopies of The Baskerville Bible and a...

source_title: From the Collection: Legacies of Swiss Style, Part 2—Wolfgang Weingart
source_description: In 1972, the editorial board of Typografische Monatsblätter (TM) , one of the leading trade journals in Switzerland, approved a series of cover designs intended to lay the groundwork for the publication’s new artistic direction. Enlisting newly appointed board member Wolfgang Weingart (1941–2021) to produce fifteen covers for the 1972 and ’73 print runs, the outcome inspired both high praise and harsh criticism from a design milieu accustomed to the quiet precision of former art director Robert Büchler (1914–2005) and regular contributor Emil Ruder (1914–1970). Weingart’s provocative covers invited an unprecedented level of controversy by appearing to flout the fundamental principles of modernist design. Instead, his iconoclastic approach struck at the very heart of the Swiss tradition. Marked by rapid advancements in phototypesetting, the early 1970s represented a transitional moment for the Swiss typographic style, as young designers began to move away from the prescriptive idealism associated with midcentury modernism. Reflecting the conditions of a globalized and increasingly turbulent world, Weingart’s work responds to a growing skepticism towards postwar optimism. Sometimes described as “Swiss Punk,” his irreverent approach provided the means to expose the limits of modern typography from within. source_title: Type West Alumni Spotlight: 2024–2025
source_description: It’s hard to believe it’s been ten years since the inaugural class of Type West (then known as Type@Cooper West) welcomed its first type design students! In 2025, we graduated 24 talented individuals from our local cohort in San Francisco and 17 other cities worldwide. The website showcasing the Class of 2025’s final typeface projects is now live! Type West Features Class of 2025 Typefaces 2019–2024 Typefaces 2021–2023 Alumni Spotlight 2019–2023 Alumni Spotlight The Archive’s collection of more than 100,000 items of graphic design and typography supports Type West’s robust curriculum, with historical examples in over 100 scripts, psychedelic gig posters from 1967’s Summer of Love, the work of contemporary artists and designers, and much more. Members of the worldwide Type West alumni community have gone on to build their own brands or release fonts through respected foundries, and quite a few have moved into educational roles to mentor the next wave of talent. Preparations are already underway to honor the past ten years of Type West with a gallery exhibition at Letterform Archive this coming fall, but we couldn’t resist this opportunity to share outstanding work by recent graduates of the program. source_title: Inside Hotel Retro : Vintage Luggage Labels Get New Life as Charming Stickers in Our Latest Book
source_description: Interior spread from Hotel Retro (left) and an example of the stickers in use (right) Hotel Retro: Vintage Luggage Labels from Tokyo to Buenos Aires (330 Travel Ephemera Stickers) Hardcover with sticker pages containing 330 removable stickers, 6.75 × 8.5 inches, 240 pages Get your copy Of the many fascinating areas in the stacks of Letterform Archive, one in particular always delights our ephemera lovers: a shelf that is home to more than half a dozen worn leather binders, filled to the brim with gorgeously designed steamer trunk labels , produced as promotions by grand hotels around the globe in the early-to-mid twentieth century. Here, the publishing team found ample inspiration for its first sticker book, Hotel Retro: Vintage Luggage Labels from Tokyo to Buenos Aires , a title replete with 330 peelable labels that readers can actually use as they were first intended: by applying them to their luggage (or whatever they like)! With a fresh book design from noted San Francisco agency MacFadden & Thorpe , the labels on view in Hotel Retro ’s pages were all selected as examples of fantastic lettering and illustration, then organized into regional chapters that demonstrate the breadth of the international trend. Printed on sophisticated uncoated paper, they have been lovingly reproduced to honor the vision of the era’s often anonymous designers. source_title: 100 Tens Celebrate a Decade of Letterform Archive
source_description: Letterform Archive is a living archive, a perpetual project to not only preserve historic design, but also inspire new work. To mark our 10th anniversary we teamed up with COLLINS to create 100 Tens : 50 interpretations of the number 1 from the Archive’s collection , paired with 50 contributions from some of the most innovative designers working today. We sent out a call to folks we admire—from type designers like Zuzana Licko and James Edmondson , to lettering artists and calligraphers like Julien Priez and Petra Dočekalová , and from graphic designers like Bráulio Amado and Marian Bantjes , to illustrators like Christoph Niemann and Susan Kare . What we got back was pure delight. The creativity and range of the submissions astounded us. All 100 Tens This gallery includes all the 10s designed by our contributors along with the objects from our collection. Click any image for a closer look, and a caption that links to the designer’s page, or the item in the Online Archive. source_title: Inside Lettres Décoratives: A Century of French Sign Painters’ Alphabets
source_description: Lettres Décoratives: A Century of French Sign Painters’ Alphabets Hardcover, 9.5 × 13 inches, 216 pages Get your copy Sometime in the 1820s, new characters arrived on the streets of France. Above boulevards, they changed color and shape across decades of urban transformation and popular revolt. Their captivating forms hailed poets into crowded cafés, embellished neighborhood shopfronts, and, for those roving city dwellers Charles Baudelaire called “botanists of the sidewalk,” turned streets into galleries as fascinating as the Louvre. Thousands of skilled painters saw to their every need. Climate and capital were hard on painted letters, always fading and displacing old signs. Two hundred years on, we sometimes struggle to appreciate their presence through black-and-white photographs and vanishing remains. Yet many have made their way to us in freshly painted glory, preserved in extraordinary nineteenth- and twentieth-century lithographic albums that share the defining alphabets of the sign painters’ trade. Lettres Décoratives: A Century of French Sign Painters’ Alphabets offers a comprehensive look inside 12 of these rare alphabet albums, sharing over 150 large-scale reproductions, together with an eye-opening historical essay by sign painting expert Morgane Côme, detailed commentary on the materials, and archival photographs of the letters in use. source_title: This Just In: Chinese Lettering Manuals, 1930⁠–⁠1971
source_description: In our ongoing effort to expand the story of graphic design beyond the Western canon, Letterform Archive continues to collect objects that illustrate the development of the world’s writing systems. This means consulting with experts in those scripts, as we recently did with Synoptic Office , a design firm working internationally with a focus on cultural heritage and archival collections. Their research into the landscape of Chinese typography appears in The Bloomsbury Handbook of Global Typography . We asked their team to source Chinese lettering manuals that are otherwise inaccessible in the West. The resulting collection, gathered from bookshops and flea markets in China, is unusual for an American institution — and one that we were unlikely to acquire any other way. In this guest post, Caspar Lam and YuJune Park of Synoptic Office tell us what they discovered. At the start of China’s Republican era in the early twentieth century, a unique form of lettering called meishuzi (美術字), or “art lettering,” 1 emerged that was distinctly different from both classical calligraphy and historically printed forms. Hastened by encounters with the West, Japanese imports, and shifting ideas about tradition and modernity, meishuzi developed alongside illustrated magazines, advertising, and the adoption of Western-style printing presses. Its newness afforded its practitioners wide latitude to experiment with novel typographic forms while retaining core ideas drawn from China’s long...
